keywords: Fine particulate matter with chemical components

papers.title: Impact of effort and expectancy on reward-related event-related potentials: Evidence from a novel effort and expectancy paradigm (EEP).
papers.abstract: Effort justification theories posit that reward is more salient after exerting effort, while effort discounting theories suggest that effort is costly and makes outcomes less salient. Reward expectation can also impact salience and influence effort and reward dynamics. To investigate the influence of both effort and expectancy of reward timing on reward-locked neural indices (i.e., RewP and P300), we created a novel monetary reward task (i.e., Effort & Expectancy Paradigm [EEP]) that modulates high and low amounts of physical effort (or passive waiting) and reward expectancy (i.e., countdown compared with no countdown trials). Eighty-two undergraduate students (61.7% female) completed surveys and the EEP during a continuous EEG recording. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to better understand the temporal and spatial subcomponents of reward-related ERPs, resulting in RewP and P300 factors. High effort trials resulted in larger RewP and P300 compared with waiting, and both the RewP and P300 were larger when reward was less expected (i.e., no countdown) compared with when reward was more expected (i.e., countdown). P300 main effects were further qualified by unique interactions between effort (press or wait), amount of effort (high or low), and expectancy (countdown or no countdown). Finally, only RewP emerged as a neural correlate of self-reported hedonic capacity. Present results suggest that salient stimuli (e.g., effortful and unexpected reward timing) enhance neural measures of reward consumption and increase allocation of cognitive resources. Reduced RewP elicited from this novel task might reflect disrupted reward processing in individuals experiencing elevated anhedonia.

papers.title: Algorithmic loops and the developing brain: a narrative review of dopaminergic mechanisms, sleep disruption, and neuroplasticity.
papers.abstract: Generation Alpha (born ~2010-2024) is the first cohort whose critical windows of dopaminergic maturation overlap entirely with mass exposure to AI-optimised short-form looping video platforms. Despite a robust epidemiological signal linking social media to depression, anxiety, attention deficits, and sleep disruption in youth, direct causal neurobiological data remain absent. This narrative review synthesises evidence from developmental neuroscience, mesolimbic dopamine physiology, sleep medicine, and longitudinal neuroimaging cohorts to articulate a mechanistic framework: chronic exposure to algorithmically engineered variable ratio reinforcement schedules may produce homeostatic D2/D3 receptor downregulation in the developing striatum, functionally analogous to the neuroadaptations observed in substance use disorders. This deficit state, characterised by anhedonia and acquired attentional dysregulation, is plausibly amplified by algorithmic disruption of slow-wave sleep-the biological window for glymphatic metabolite clearance and synaptic homeostasis. Converging evidence from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study documents associations between screen behaviour and grey matter volume, reward-circuit activation, and executive function trajectories across early adolescence. Because direct in vivo measurement of D2 receptor density in children using PET radioligands is ethically prohibited, we propose a cross-species, multimodal longitudinal research framework. This integrates a novel nonhuman primate digital self-administration paradigm with human cohort studies utilising computational phenotyping of algorithmic dosage, polysomnographic sleep monitoring, and annual reward-task fMRI. Current evidence justifies both urgent regulatory action and a dedicated research programme to characterise the neurobiological consequences of a uniquely 21st-century exposure.

papers.title: A canonical microcircuit for estimating Excitation/Inhibition (E/I) balance.
papers.abstract: Excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance is crucial for maintaining healthy brain function and can be disrupted in various neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite its importance, there are few tools to study E/I balance non-invasively in humans. Here, we propose a canonical microcircuit model to estimate E/I balance from non-invasive magnetoencephalography (MEG), electroencephalography (EEG) or optically pumped magnetometers (OPM) recordings by parameterising global pyramidal and inhibitory cell excitability. We first establish that E/I parameters are identifiable and recoverable. We then explore the effects of these new parameters and their interaction with other parameters in a series of simulations. To highlight the clinical relevance of this new model, we simulate changes in E/I balance and their impact on event-related potentials (ERPs) derived from paired-click, passive and active oddball paradigms, which are among the most robust clinical biomarkers of schizophrenia. Our simulations show that a loss of pyramidal cell excitability can explain reduced ERP amplitudes across all three paradigms, mirroring empirical findings in schizophrenia. This method may serve as a computational assay for estimating synaptopathy and E/I balance from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings across various clinical conditions thereby advancing efforts to develop personalised interventions to restore E/I balance.

papers.title: Digital health information-seeking behavior correlates of parental cyberchondria severity in Pediatric care.
papers.abstract: Limited evidence addresses whether digital health information-seeking behaviors are independently associated with parental cyberchondria in pediatric settings. We examined these associations after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics and psychological well-being. This cross-sectional study was conducted in the pediatric ward of a hospital in eastern Türkiye from August 2024 to January 2025 using convenience sampling. Eligible participants were adults accompanying a child aged 0-18 years who could consent and complete the questionnaire. Of 482 invited parents, 27 declined and 455 completed a self-administered questionnaire in the child's room. Hierarchical linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors included 451 complete cases. The 16 item-level indicators increased explained variance by 50.0 percentage points (ΔR2 = 0.500, p < .001); the final model explained 57.6% (adjusted R2 = 0.553). Higher scores were associated with reliance on non-health-professional rather than health-professional sources (B = 3.531, 95% CI [0.340, 6.721], p = .030), greater search frequency (B = 1.771, 95% CI [0.909, 2.633], p < .001), pre-hospital searching (B = 3.412, p = .002), increased worry about the child's health (B = 2.952, p = .004), and sleep pattern disruption (B = 3.617, p < .001). Digital health information-seeking behaviors were associated with parental cyberchondria severity. These findings, derived from parents of children receiving care in a pediatric clinical setting, may inform health-informatics-supported pediatric nursing care by providing insight into parents' digital health information-seeking experiences and related communication needs. Causality cannot be inferred because of the cross-sectional design. No patients or members of the public were involved in the design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, or reporting of this study. Parents participated only as questionnaire respondents.

papers.title: Editorial: Supporting the mental health of neurodivergent adults through sleep and circadian based interventions.
papers.abstract: Autistic, ADHD and AuDHD adults frequently experience sleep/circadian disruptions that impact their mental health. There is, however, a lack of effective and scalable interventions tailored for these groups that can address their treatment needs in this area. In this editorial, we summarise the challenge and propose a programme of basic science research that can inform the development of suitable interventions. We emphasise the importance of a co-design approach and of combining objective and subjective sleep/circadian measurement with mental health symptom data longitudinally to illuminate the within-person relations between sleep/circadian function and mental health. We highlight the need to better understand the sleep/circadian profiles of AuDHD individuals and their implications for mental health as a particularly critical gap.

papers.title: Evaluation of the management of patients with suspected epileptic seizures in emergency departments: The EPI-Lepsie study.
papers.abstract: In France, epileptic seizures account for approximately 1.6% of emergency department (ED) admissions, nearly 60% of which involve patients with known epilepsy. At least half of these patients could potentially be managed on an outpatient basis. Despite established national guidelines, data on actual ED practice patterns and guideline adherence remain scarce. To evaluate the management of adult patients presenting with suspected epileptic seizures across French EDs, and to identify clinical and organisational determinants of hospitalisation. The EPI-Lepsie study was a national, multicentre, prospective observational study. Consecutive adult patients (age≥18 years) admitted to 93 French EDs over a three-day period (18-21 May 2021) with suspected epileptic seizures were enrolled through the Initiative Recherche Urgence (IRU) network of the Société française de médecine d'urgence (SFMU). The primary outcome was hospitalisation at ED discharge. Secondary outcomes included EEG performance, access to neurological consultation, post-discharge follow-up, and 30-day outcomes. Hospitalisation determinants were assessed by mixed logistic regression (ED as random intercept), adjusted for age, sex, seizure aetiology, risk factors, neuroimaging, and EEG results. Among 350 included patients (61.8% male; median age 50 years [IQR: 33-68]), EEG was requested in 102 cases (29.1%) but performed in only 54 (15.4%). Neurological consultation was requested in 163 patients (46.6%) and obtained in 146 (41.7%). After ED care, 210 patients (60.2%) were discharged home, of whom 133 (66.5%) had no scheduled neurological follow-up. Hospitalisation occurred in 128 patients (36.6%). In multivariate analysis, abnormal neuroimaging was the strongest independent predictor (adjusted OR 8.70, P<0.0001). Failure to perform a requested EEG was associated with hospitalisation in 81.2% of cases versus 46.3% when EEG was completed. Inter-centre variance accounted for 19.9% of total variance. This study demonstrates that a substantial proportion of epilepsy-related ED admissions do not require hospitalisation. Improving access to EEG and neurological consultation, combined with standardised risk-stratification pathways for patients with known epilepsy, could meaningfully reduce avoidable admissions and enhance continuity of care.

papers.title: Interactions between daytime sleep and nighttime sleep at 5 and 17 months: Factors from a representative post-pandemic epidemiological cohort.
papers.abstract: Associations between daytime and nighttime sleep remain poorly documented in early infancy, a developmental period during which sleep patterns are still consolidating. This study aims to (1) examine the prospective associations between daytime and nighttime sleep duration, and (2) identify child, maternal and environmental characteristics associated with daytime and nighttime sleep duration at 17 months of age. Maternal reports for 3873 infants from the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development (2021-2023) were collected at 5 months (T1) and 17 months (T2) in a post-pandemic population-based cohort. Cross-lagged regression models were conducted using MPlus; associations with P < .01 are reported. The cross-sectional relations between daytime and nighttime sleep were negative at both T1 (P = .01) and T2 (P < .001). Longer daytime and nighttime sleep at T1 were both associated with longer nighttime sleep at T2 (P < .001). Longer daytime sleep at T1 was associated with longer daytime sleep at T2 (P < .001). However, longer nighttime sleep T1 was not associated with longer daytime sleep at T2. Higher maternal educational attainment, maternal immigrant status, and being a boy were associated with longer daytime sleep at T2. A broader set of maternal and environmental factors, such as younger maternal age, maternal immigrant status, higher weekly screen time at T2, and lower household income were associated with shorter nighttime sleep at T2. These results highlight the importance of supporting developmentally appropriate sleep opportunities and addressing contextual factors that may shape early sleep health.

papers.title: Dexmedetomidine produces more sleep-like brain activity compared with propofol in human participants. Response to Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 1217-8.

Hypothalamic Neurochemical and Microglial Suppression in Long-Standing Human Hibernation-Like Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Seasonally recurring hibernation-like states are exceptionally rare in humans, and their neural substrates remain unknown. We investigated the brain of a 57-year-old woman with a > 30-year history of winter-associated hypothermia, neuroendocrine instability, psychomotor suppression and circannual rhythmicity. Postmortem neuropathological analysis revealed preserved hypothalamic and basal forebrain anatomy but profound neurochemical abnormalities. Key peptidergic neuronal populations involved in circadian and neuroendocrine regulation, including arginine vasopressin (AVP), oxytocin (OXT), corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) neurons, showed near-complete loss of immunoreactivity in the SCN, SON and PVN. Immunoreactivity for vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and neurotensin (NT) in the SCN was markedly reduced. These changes were accompanied by markedly reduced synaptophysin immunoreactivity in all hypothalamic regions examined, whereas catecholaminergic neurons were relatively preserved in the PVN and SON. Beyond the hypothalamus, cholinergic neurons in the NBM showed a moderate reduction without evidence of Alzheimer-related pathology. Microglial immunoreactivity was nearly absent in the hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic regions examined, contrasting with preserved GFAP and AQP4 immunoreactivity. Moreover, myelination and microvascular architecture also remained intact. These findings identify a selective hypothalamic and microglial suppression associated with a rare human hibernation-like phenotype and indicate markedly reduced output of core neuroendocrine and circadian circuits during long-standing hypometabolic states. The case also illustrates that recurrent, profound hypothermia can be tolerated over decades without systemic organ failure, highlighting an unexpected degree of human metabolic resilience.

papers.title: Fatigue Characteristics and Perceptions in US Helicopter Air Ambulance Pilots.
papers.abstract: Helicopter air ambulance (HAA) operations involve shiftwork schedules that put personnel at an increased risk of fatigue. This survey study aimed to provide an updated benchmark for fatigue characteristics and perceptions within US HAA pilots. Pilots across the US HAA industry were invited to complete a survey related to their work and individual sleep-related preferences. Pilots completed the survey, including standardized questionnaires such as the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, during a larger field study. Our survey of 120 pilots across 21 operators revealed that poor self-reported sleep quality is an issue in more than half (53%) of the sample population. Most participants (71%) felt that fatigue was most prevalent on the return-to-base leg of a trip, and 69% felt that the number of flight requests was the greatest schedule-related contributor to fatigue. One-third of the pilots (34%) reported "nodding off" during a flight, and more than three-quarters (87%) said that their work performance had been affected by sleep inertia. The pilots provided suggestions as to how to mitigate fatigue risk through flight request limits, duty duration maximums, and sleep inertia protections. Overall, the results of this survey can be used to identify areas of fatigue risk to be addressed through operational policies and to highlight areas in need of further research.

Visuospatial attention modulates audiovisual temporal perception: Context-dependent associations between prestimulus alpha lateralization and perceptual reports.
papers.abstract: Audiovisual temporal perception depends on the timing of sensory events and on preparatory attention. We examined how visuospatial cueing affects explicit synchrony judgments and sound-induced flash illusions, and how prestimulus EEG relates to these perceptual reports. In Experiment 1 (N = 39), participants judged beep-flash synchrony across auditory- and visual-leading stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). In Experiment 2 (N = 36), they reported flashes in fusion and fission conditions across SOAs and corresponding references. Experiment 1 showed a Cue validity × SOA interaction, with more synchrony reports on valid trials at -100 and +50 ms. Cueing shifted the point of subjective simultaneity among 21 participants with reliable fits. Trial-level posterior alpha lateralization was associated with synchrony reports as a function of Cue validity. In Experiment 2, valid cues reduced raw fusion reports at -100, -50, and +100 ms. A Cue validity × SOA interaction persisted for reference-adjusted fusion scores, whereas neither raw nor adjusted fission showed a corresponding interaction. The association between reference-adjusted alpha lateralization and fusion reports varied with Cue validity and SOA, although a direct comparison with the visual reference did not establish an illusion-specific association. These EEG-behavior associations were stable after accounting for temporal progression, preceding trials, cue side, and an ocular-sensitive EEG proxy. Together, the findings indicate timing- and context-dependent effects of visuospatial attention on audiovisual temporal perception and identify preparatory posterior alpha lateralization as a correlate of subsequent reports.

papers.title: Sleep Disorders in Patients with Systemic Sclerosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background : Systemic sclerosis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with substantial morbidity and reduced quality of life. Sleep disturbance has been reported with variable frequency in patients with systemic sclerosis, though its prevalence remains incompletely characterised. Objective : This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of sleep disorders in patients with systemic sclerosis. Methods : Six databases were searched up to 15 February 2026 without language restriction. Studies reporting sleep outcomes in adults with systemic sclerosis were eligible. Prevalence estimates were pooled using a logit transformation with a random-effects model and Hartung-Knapp correction. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Publication bias was evaluated with Egger's test and the trim-and-fill method. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251152354). Results : Twenty-three studies totalling 1,487 patients were included across all analyses. Eleven studies (820 patients) contributed to the primary meta-analysis of poor sleep quality assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. The pooled prevalence of poor sleep quality was 76.49% (95% CI 66.62 to 84.13%), with moderate to substantial heterogeneity (I² = 70.1%) and a 95% prediction interval of 49.66% to 91.47%, indicating that the true prevalence may range from approximately half to nearly all patients across different SSc populations. Five studies (346 patients) contributed to the obstructive sleep apnea meta-analysis, yielding a pooled prevalence of 40.30% (95% CI 25.56 to 57.04%, I² = 71.8%) with a 95% prediction interval of 13.95% to 73.75%. Five additional studies were included in a qualitative synthesis only, and three randomised controlled trials addressed sleep interventions. Egger's test identified possible funnel plot asymmetry. After trim-and-fill adjustment, four studies were imputed and the corrected estimate was 69.62% (95% CI 57.33 to 79.63%), somewhat lower than the primary estimate, suggesting that the primary estimate may be modestly influenced by publication bias. The certainty of evidence was rated as low according to GRADE. Conclusion : Available evidence suggests that sleep disorders may affect approximately three quarters of patients with systemic sclerosis when assessed by the PSQI, and obstructive sleep apnea may affect more than one third when evaluated by objective tools. These estimates carry low GRADE certainty and wide prediction intervals, and should not be interpreted as definitive prevalence figures. Larger prospective studies and well-powered randomised trials are needed to establish more precise estimates and to evaluate targeted sleep interventions in this population.

papers.title: Are Cannabis and Cannabinoids a Valid Treatment Option in Patients with Rheumatic Diseases? A narrative review.
papers.abstract: To evaluate current evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of cannabis and cannabinoids in patients with rheumatic diseases. A narrative review was conducted based on a search for studies published between 2000 and 2026 evaluating cannabinoid therapies in rheumatic diseases. We identified 17 preclinical studies on the mechanisms of action of cannabis and 43 clinical studies published between 2000 and 2026, including randomized trials, observational studies and systematic reviews. We identified two articles on rheumatoid arthritis, 10 on osteoarthritis (2 reviews and 8 clinical studies), 28 on fibromyalgia (9 reviews, 7 randomized control trials, 12 clinical studies), one on psoriatic arthritis, and one on systemic sclerosis. The evidence of an effect of cannabinoids was strongest for fibromyalgia and limited for rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Most studies reported improvements in pain and sleep quality. Globally, cannabinoids were well tolerated. Some studies suggest short-term symptomatic benefits of cannabinoid-based therapies, particularly in fibromyalgia, but the findings are inconsistent and limited by small samples, heterogeneous formulations, and risk of bias. Current evidence is insufficient to support routine clinical use or recommendations in rheumatic diseases.

papers.title: Total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves improve sleep quality in mice with perimenopausal insomnia and are associated with altered expression of 5-HT1AR, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2.
papers.abstract: Hemerocallis citrina Baroni has a long history of dietary and medicinal use in China. Its dried whole herb is documented as an ethnic medicinal material in the 2003 edition of the Guizhou Provincial Quality Standards for Chinese Medicinal and Ethnic Medicinal Materials, while Hemerocallis flowers are traditionally used for "ye shao an mei" (), referring to reduced or disturbed sleep at night. Modern studies have demonstrated sleep-improving effects of the flowers, and previous work showed neuroprotective and antidepressant-like activities of total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves (HLTP). However, the effects of HLTP on perimenopausal insomnia (PMI) remain unclear. To evaluate the effects of HLTP on sleep disturbances in mice exhibiting perimenopausal and insomnia-like features and investigate associated molecular changes. HLTP was prepared using a previously reported procedure. Network pharmacology predicted candidate targets and pathways for 32 phenolic constituents identified in an earlier HLTP batch, while molecular docking assessed predicted binding to 10 core targets selected by protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis. A composite mouse model was generated using 4-vinylcyclohexene dioxide (VCD) to induce perimenopausal features, followed by para-chloro-DL-phenylalanine (PCPA) to induce insomnia-like disturbances. Seventy female C57BL/6J mice were randomized into seven groups (n = 10 per group): Control, Con+HLTP, Model, HLTP-L/M/H (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, respectively), and zopiclone. Treatment began with model induction. Behavioral tests, pentobarbital-induced sleep testing, 24 h electroencephalographic/electromyographic (EEG/EMG) polysomnography, histopathology, biochemical assays, and Western blotting were used to evaluate pharmacological effects and associated molecular changes. 16S rRNA sequencing, serum untargeted metabolomics, and brain transcriptomics were additionally performed to characterize complementary changes in the gut microbiota, systemic metabolism, and central gene expression. Network pharmacology prioritized the serotonergic synapse pathway for further investigation. HLTP improved behavioral and sleep-related abnormalities, with the most consistent effects at the high dose. EEG/EMG polysomnography showed a partial shift in sleep-wake distribution toward the Control pattern. During the inactive phase, high-dose HLTP shortened non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep latencies, reduced Wake bout number and NREM-to-Wake transitions, prolonged NREM bout duration, and increased NREM sleep time (P < 0.05). HLTP also attenuated neuronal morphological abnormalities and improved sex hormone, monoamine neurotransmitter, oxidative stress, and inflammatory indicators. Western blotting showed increased expression of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A receptor (5-HT1AR) and gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor α2 subunit (GABRA2), together with decreased expression of adenylyl cyclase 5 (ADCY5) and protein kinase A (PKA) after HLTP treatment. Multi-omics analyses revealed changes in gut microbial composition, serum metabolism, and brain gene expression following HLTP treatment. Pathway enrichment analysis of exploratory candidate metabolites identified FDR-supported enrichment of steroid biosynthesis. Brain transcriptomics identified FDR-supported enrichment of circadian rhythm in the Model vs. Control comparison and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction in the HLTP-H vs. Model comparison. None of the tested cross-omics correlations remained significant after FDR correction. HLTP ameliorated sleep disturbances in mice subjected to the VCD+PCPA composite model, accompanied by improvements in neuroendocrine indicators and changes in 5-HT1AR, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2 protein expression. The omics findings provided complementary exploratory evidence, although the functional relationships among these changes remain to be established.

papers.title: Distinct whole-brain c-Fos expression mapping following acute and chronic partial sleep deprivation in mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep loss constitutes a major health challenge, encompassing both acute sleep deprivation (ASD) and chronic partial sleep deprivation (CPSD). However, the differential impact of ASD and CPSD on brain-wide neuronal activity remains poorly understood. Here, we employed high-definition fluorescent micro-optical sectioning tomography (HD-fMOST) coupled with automated c-Fos quantification to systematically map global c-Fos expression in mice subjected to ASD, post-ASD recovery sleep (ASR), and CPSD. We found that 6 h of ASD broadly upregulated c-Fos expression, which was largely restored by 2 h of ASR. In contrast, 2 wk. of CPSD predominantly suppressed c-Fos but induced complex regional disparities. Cluster analysis delineated distinct activation patterns at the brain network level, whereas across conditions, similar trends were commonly observed in regions subserving related physiological functions. These findings reveal distinct whole-brain neuronal activation profiles following acute versus chronic sleep loss, highlighting potential neuromodulatory targets for treating sleep deprivation-induced dysfunction.

papers.title: Perivascular space imaging marker and glymphatic function in obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a recognized cardiovascular and dementia risk factor that has been previously reported in association with enlarged cerebral perivascular spaces (PVS) indicative of cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) and impaired glymphatic function. We aimed to evaluate associations between OSA and neuroimaging-visible PVS and Diffusion Tensor Imaging Analysis Along the Perivascular Space (DTI-ALPS), as a surrogate marker of glymphatic function. A systematic search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Embase was conducted through Oct 11, 2026. The meta-analysis included observational studies exploring associations between OSA severity and PVS burden and DTI-ALPS. Reported effect estimates for PVS or glymphatic parameters across OSA disease severity were pooled using a random-effect model. Sixteen studies (N = 2618) met the inclusion criteria. Results showed that patients with OSA had a significantly higher odds of documented PVS compared to those without OSA (OR = 4.97, 95% CI 2.51 to 9.82). Each per unit increase in apnea-hypopnea index corresponded to a 3% increase in the odds of PVS (OR = 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.04). OSA was linked to a significant decrease in glymphatic-related diffusion as indicated by DTI-ALPS index (mean difference = -0.2, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.06). This reduction persisted across all OSA severities, including mild (mean difference = -0.17, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.02), and moderate-to-severe (mean difference = -0.10, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.04) OSA. Our meta-analysis demonstrated a strong link between OSA and both increased PVS burden and impaired surrogate of glymphatic function, potentially implicating OSA in the pathogenesis of both CSVD and dementia. Further prospective studies are necessary to confirm causality and direction of effect of the observed association. Registration PROSPERO registration number, CRD420261279540. ABBREVIATIONS AND ACRONYMS.

papers.title: The Mouse Retina as an Evolving Model System: From Layered Anatomy to Cell-Type-Resolved Regenerative Repair.
papers.abstract: The mouse retina has become a central model for linking neural organization to degeneration and repair because it combines laminated anatomy, genetic access, longitudinal imaging, and measurable visual function. This review is organized around three methodological eras: anatomical foundations (1970s-1990s), genetic access and reproducible injury models (2000s-2010s), and cell-resolved omics and high-resolution in vivo imaging (2015-present). Four Method Boxes translate this history into practical guidance for histology, electrophysiology, genetic manipulation, and in vivo imaging. We then examine two therapeutic areas that expose the model's evidentiary limits: retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axon regeneration after optic nerve injury and stage-matched treatment of photoreceptor degeneration. Across both areas, survival, local function, long-distance regeneration, circuit reconnection, and behavior are treated as distinct outcomes. The mouse retina is therefore most informative when complementary readouts are combined and promising mechanisms are tested against human-relevant tissue and larger-eye systems before clinical inference.

papers.title: Psychosocial and symptom burden across metabolic populations managed in a digitally enabled metabolic care model: a real-world cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Psychosocial screening is growing in diabetes care, however, its role in broader metabolic populations remains unclear. This study aimed to describe patient-reported psychosocial outcomes and their associations with cardiometabolic characteristics in individuals managed through a digitally enabled hybrid care model. This retrospective cross-sectional study included adults at Metabolic (United Arab Emirates) enrolled between September 2024 and December 2025. Patients were categorized into diabetic (DM), non-diabetic metabolic (NDM), and overweight-obesity focused (OB) cohorts. Scores for various psychosocial tools were recomputed from item-level responses, and biochemical measures were extracted from medical records. Associations were examined with multivariable logistic regression. Of 7,449 patients, 937 (12.6%) had DM, 5,594 (75.1%) had NDM, and 918 (12.3%) had OB. High risk for obstructive sleep apnea was present in 49.8% of DM, 27.7% of NDM, and 32.4% of OB patients. Depressive symptoms were reported similarly in DM (25.6%) and NDM (23.5%); anxiety symptoms were also comparable across groups. Diabetes distress affected 50.6% of DM patients. HbA1c correlated with PAID-5 distress, and BMI was associated with various psychosocial outcomes; discrimination was modest (AUC 0.55-0.67). Conclusion Depressive and anxiety symptoms were prevalent in both non-diabetic and those with diabetes, suggesting the need for structured screening beyond diabetes.

papers.title: Clinical, neurophysiological, and radiological correlates of treatment response in elderly patients with epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy in elderly patients presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, with variable clinical, neuroimaging, and electroencephalographic (EEG) features. Understanding these complexities is crucial for optimizing management strategies in this growing population. To characterize the clinical, neuroimaging, and EEG features of elderly-onset epilepsy and to evaluate their association with seizure control and treatment response. We retrospectively evaluated 37 epilepsy cases with seizure onset after 65-years-old who had been followed up at a tertiary care center between January 2019 and January 2023. Clinical characteristics, EEG and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, seizure types, treatment responses, and comorbidities were systematically analyzed. Seizure syndromes were classified according to International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) criteria. Structural focal and unknown etiology epilepsy were the most common subtypes. Seizure remission for at least 36 consecutive months was achieved in 81.1% of patients, with 64.9% responding to first-line antiseizure therapy. The MRI scan revealed epileptogenic lesions in 40.5% of patients; however, no statistically significant association was found between neuroimaging findings and treatment outcomes. Some EEG abnormalities were noted, including epileptiform discharges (24.3%) and background slowing (24.3%), but no statistically significant association was found with seizure control. Convulsive status epilepticus occurred in 10.8% of patients but was generally well-managed. Psychiatric comorbidities were encountered less frequently compared with younger populations. Comprehensive clinical assessment, supported by neurophysiological and radiological findings, may help optimize the diagnosis and effective management of epilepsy in elderly patients.

papers.title: Zika-Related Microcephaly in the First 5 Years After Birth.
papers.abstract: To characterize clinical manifestations and complications of children with Zika-related microcephaly in the first 5 years after birth. A cohort of children with Zika-related microcephaly were observed up to age 60 months as part of the Microcephaly Epidemic Research Group Pediatric Cohort. Among the 181 children, 43.1% were male and 77.2% were born at term. The median birth weight was 2700 g, with 64.8% classified as small for gestational age. Notably, 22.3% were diagnosed with microcephaly after birth, and 48.8% had severe microcephaly. Most common phenotypic characteristics were craniofacial disproportion (54.1%), arthrogryposis (35.9%), and exacerbated occipital protuberance (35.5%). Approximately one-third (33.1%) presented with dysphagia (n = 151 evaluated at median age of 28.2 months), and 13.3% of children had gastrostomies (median age of 24 months). Hearing anomalies were detected in 9.7% (n = 93 evaluated at median age of 30 months). In ophthalmological evaluation, 30.4% showed changes in the retina and 28.5% in the optic nerve; strabismus was observed in 53.4%. During neurological assessment (median age at first assessment of 15.9 months), 73.8% presented with abnormalities. Imaging examinations showed ventriculomegaly and cortical atrophy in 75.3% and 64.4% of the children, respectively. Electroencephalography was performed based on clinical indication in 84 children, of whom 92.9% had pattern alterations. Over the 5 years, 62.4% were hospitalized, mainly for respiratory problems and seizures. The study highlights the severity of Zika-related microcephaly. Future research should prioritize continued systematic monitoring of these children to understand the frequency and timing of late-onset manifestations and complications, including death.

papers.title: Postpartum mice display distinct behavioral and neuroimmune responses to chronic circadian disruption.
papers.abstract: The maternal brain undergoes profound adaptations during peripartum to support offspring development and maternal wellbeing. These adaptations are partly coordinated by neuroimmune signaling, including changes in the density and activity of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Microglia are regulated by the circadian system, which coordinates cellular activity across 24-h cycles, and disruption of circadian timing can alter neuroimmune activity and mood-related behaviors. Maternal rhythms are disrupted by offspring care demands; however, how such disruption affects maternal behavior, mood, and neuroimmune function remains unclear. We hypothesized that postpartum females would show greater behavioral and neuroimmune sensitivity to chronic circadian disruption than nulliparous controls. To test this, mice underwent a chronic phase advancement (CPA) paradigm (six-hour phase advance every four days) from postnatal days (P) 0-18 with behavioral testing occurring at an acute (P2-3) and chronic (P14-17) timepoint. Contrary to our prediction, maternal nest building and pup retrieval were maintained in mice after a single-phase shift. Sucrose preference was reduced by phase shifts at both the acute and chronic timepoint, but this reduction was comparable between parous and nulliparous females, showing no distinction based on parity. However, chronic CPA produced parity-dependent effects on behavior: CPA increased grooming and reduced nest preference in parous mice. In the medial preoptic area (MPOA), a brain region critical for maternal behavior, CPA reduced microglia density in parous compared to nulliparous females. MPOA transcriptomic analysis further showed parity × CPA interaction effects on synapse organization and RNA processing pathways. Chronic circadian disruption, therefore, shifts postpartum behavior, neuroimmune activity, and MPOA gene expression, in a distinct manner from nulliparous controls. Elucidating circadian-neuroimmune interactions in the postpartum brain may reveal novel targets for circadian-based interventions for postpartum mood disorders.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal immune remodeling by light at night uncovers an adaptive immune signature linked to tumor progression and anti-PD-1 non-response.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption, notably induced by light at night (LAN), is increasingly recognized as a modulator of systemic immune function; however, its high-resolution spatiotemporal impact and relevance to cancer immunotherapy remain poorly defined. Here, we constructed a spatiotemporal single-cell transcriptomic atlas of murine lymph nodes, peripheral blood, and spleen across circadian time points to dissect the immunological consequences of LAN exposure. We observed that LAN exposure was associated with profound, tissue-specific transcriptional remodeling of the adaptive immune system. Specifically, B cells exhibited suppressed circadian clock programs and impaired homing and retention signatures. Concurrently, CD8+ T cells exhibited transcriptional profiles consistent with an aberrantly activated, late-effector state, a transition accompanied by altered intercellular MHC-I communication. To evaluate the translational relevance of these transcriptomic shifts, we developed a computational LAN Immune Dyssynchrony Score (LAN-IDS) and projected these murine-derived signatures onto human cancer cohorts. In human melanoma sentinel lymph nodes, the LAN-associated CD8+ T cell trajectory exhibited strong directional concordance with advanced (Stage III) disease. Crucially, interrogating these signatures within a clinical melanoma cohort revealed that the aberrantly activated CD8+ T cell program is significantly elevated in patients with primary resistance to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy. Collectively, our cross-species computational analysis identifies a spatiotemporal adaptive immune dyssynchrony signature. These findings identify specific lymphocyte transcriptional states that may serve as candidate correlates of tumor progression and immunotherapy non-response.

papers.title: Effect of voclosporin on psychiatric disorders: real-world pharmacovigilance and genetic evidence.
papers.abstract: Voclosporin, a novel oral calcineurin inhibitor (CNI), is increasingly used in clinical practice. The relationship between voclosporin and psychiatric disorders remains unclear. Adverse events (AEs) associated with voclosporin were extracted from the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database, covering the period from first quarter of 2021 to the third quarter of 2024. Disproportionality analysis including reporting odds ratio (ROR) and Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) was employed to identify potential psychotic safety signals associated with voclosporin. Furthermore, drug target Mendelian randomization (MR) was utilized to assess the causal association between voclosporin and psychiatric disorders. A total of 313 cases of psychiatric disorders associated with voclosporin were recorded among 260 patients. In the pharmacovigilance analysis, insomnia (N = 64, ROR = 1.39, 95% CI: 1.09-1.77) emerged as the most frequently reported psychiatric disorders and showed a positive signal. Specifically, the insomnia signal for voclosporin is more pronounced than that of traditional CNIs, and persists despite restriction to indications (SLE and LN) and other CNIs as control groups. In the drug target MR analysis, genetically predicted voclosporin was associated with a higher risk of insomnia (OR=1.37,95%CI:1.16-1.62, P < 0.001) and sleep disorder (OR=1.64,95%CI:1.17-2.29, P = 0.004). This study underscores a positive correlation between voclosporin and increased insomnia. Physicians should pay more attention to insomnia during administering voclosporin and implement timely measures such as monitoring sleep quality, adjusting drug dosages or treatment regimens, or adding insomnia agents.

papers.title: Theta-frequency sensory entrainment promotes episodic memory consolidation.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations in the theta frequency range have been implicated in episodic memory processes. Previous work using EEG neurofeedback and non-invasive brain stimulation has demonstrated that enhancing theta activity immediately after encoding can improve long-term memory retention. The present study examined whether audio-visual entrainment combined with cranio-electro stimulation (AVE + CES), a noninvasive and accessible method, may similarly support early stages of consolidation. Sixty-nine undergraduate participants were assigned to one of three oscillatory sensory entrainment conditions: Theta 3 Hz and Theta 5.5 Hz (to examine frequency-specific theta effects), or Beta 16 Hz (as a control condition). Participants completed three study-test cycles of an episodic free-recall task, followed by 20 min of AVE + CES during which they were exposed to rhythmically flashing lights, pulsing tones, and mild earlobe electrical stimulation. Memory performance was assessed immediately after entrainment, after 24 h, and after one week. Baseline-corrected retention scores were computed relative to pre-entrainment performance. No group differences were observed prior to entrainment and baseline-corrected retention did not differ between groups immediately following entrainment. However, both theta groups exhibited significantly reduced forgetting relative to the beta group after 24 h and one week, with no differences between the two theta frequencies. These findings suggest that theta-frequency sensory entrainment broadly enhances episodic memory consolidation, highlighting AVE + CES as a promising and accessible approach for promoting mnemonic retention.

papers.title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
papers.abstract: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks. Prospective study. and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported. Elite youth athletes. Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042). Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.
papers.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine

papers.title: Two cases of hydranencephaly with epileptic spasms: New insights from fast oscillation analysis of scalp EEG.
papers.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology

papers.title: Developmental sleep during lethargus is associated with metabolic homeostasis and heritable adaptive responses to infection in Caenorhabditis elegans.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental physiological state essential for metabolic and neuronal homeostasis; however, its contribution to lipid and energy metabolism during development remains incompletely understood. Here, we used Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the metabolic significance of Developmentally Timed Sleep (DTS). Lethargus-associated DTS was mechanically disrupted using 1 kHz piezoelectric buzzer-induced mechanical stimulation, followed by behavioural, physiological, metabolic and molecular analyses. DTS disruption was associated with reduced behavioural quiescence, altered sleep-associated gene expression, reduced survival and elevated oxidative stress. Notably, disruption during the L4-young adult lethargus window was associated with increased feeding and markedly enhanced lipid accumulation, accompanied by upregulation of the lipid metabolic regulators fat-6, nhr-64 and nhr-80. Despite increased lipid storage, levels of the triglyceride lipase ATGL were elevated, suggesting enhanced lipid mobilization concurrent with persistent lipid accumulation. This metabolic phenotype was accompanied by reduced mitochondrial activity, decreased intracellular ATP, downregulation of atp-3 and activation of AMPK-mediated energy sensing, suggesting energetic stress and potentially inefficient downstream utilization of mobilized lipids. DTS disruption was additionally associated with increased acy-1 and crh-1 expression and enhanced CREB phosphorylation, indicating altered cAMP-CREB-associated neuronal signalling. Furthermore, disruption of DTS in offspring of Salmonella Typhi-infected parents was associated with reduction in their ability to generate heritable adaptive resistance and altered daf-16, sgk-1 and skn-1 mRNA expression. Collectively, these findings suggest that developmental sleep may play a role in lipid storage, mobilization, mitochondrial bioenergetics and cellular energy sensing, with potential consequences for neuronal and adaptive stress responses.

papers.title: Age- and noise-related differences in neural entrainment to speech sounds.
papers.abstract: Speech-in-noise (SIN) perception is a difficult everyday listening task that becomes more difficult with age. Neural tracking of target speech is associated with successful speech perception in clean and noise-degraded listening environments. How aging impacts neural tracking of speech and behavioral decrements in SIN perception remains unclear. To address these questions, we measured neural speech tracking during a continuous SIN perception task in younger and older adults via multichannel electroencephalography (EEG). Participants (N = 83) monitored a continuous stream of syllables (~4.5 Hz) presented in quiet and noise conditions during EEG recordings. We assessed neural phase-locking value (PLV) to the acoustic speech envelope to investigate interactions between aging, hearing loss, and stimulus noise on neural synchronization to speech. Compared to younger adults, older adults demonstrated less behavioral sensitivity to noise effects than young adults and had higher overall PLV to target speech. Older adults also showed greater noise-related degradations in neural speech processing relative to younger listeners. Age remained a strong predictor of behavioral responses to speech even after controlling for hearing loss. Covarying for hearing loss removed most age-related effects on neural PLV. Older adults demonstrate exaggerated neural tracking to ongoing speech presented in quiet and greater noise-related reductions in neurobehavioral speech processing than young adults. Our results support the decline-compensation hypothesis, corroborate unusually large speech envelope encoding in older listeners, and suggest more robust neural synchronization to the speech signal is not always perceptually advantageous.

papers.title: Assessing brain-behaviour coupling in non-invasive brain stimulation: Insights from reliable change indices and Monte Carlo simulations.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NiBS) studies frequently report exploratory brain-behaviour correlations following the application of NiBS. However, these analyses are typically underpowered and rely on ratio-based change scores with known statistical limitations. We addressed these limitations by pooling individual data from three independent studies (N = 69) and combining empirical analysis with a Monte Carlo simulation framework. All studies applied 20 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) targeting the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG) during a stop signal task. Changes in preSMA-rIFG EEG imaginary coherency (ImCoh) and stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) were quantified using reliable change indices (RCI), z-standardised within studies for pooled mixed-effects regression. We found no meaningful association between tACS-induced ImCoh change and SSRT change (r = .013, marginal R2 = .004), with project-wise correlations being small, non-significant, and directionally inconsistent. While sensitivity analysis using ratio-based change scores converged on the same null result (r = .014), the simulation framework revealed that ratio-based scores show near-complete failure to recover true brain-behaviour associations across all plausible effect sizes. Conversely, RCI-based scores preserved directional accuracy and provided well-calibrated Type I error control, despite moderate attenuation under realistic noise conditions. These results highlight the severe statistical limits of detecting individual-level brain-behaviour coupling following 20 Hz tACS. Rather than ruling out a true biological association, our findings demonstrate that standard sample sizes and typical measurement noise create substantial 'blindness' to realistic effect sizes, underscoring a broader need for more reliable metrics and adequately powered designs in NiBS research.
papers.journal: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior

papers.title: The effect of physical activity timing on insomnia and sleep quality: a randomized cross-over trial in older adults.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms are common in older adults. While observational studies suggest physical activity (PA) timing affects health outcomes, its effect on sleep remains unclear. We compared morning versus evening PA effects on insomnia severity and sleep quality in older adults with insomnia symptoms. Eligible participants were aged 60-80 years with (sub)clinical insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index [ISI] score ≥10). In a randomized cross-over trial, participants engaged in coached PA in the morning (10:00-11:00) or evening (19:30-20:30) for 14 days each. ISI scores were assessed post-intervention. Objective sleep parameters-duration, latency, efficiency, and timing-were assessed with a Withings Sleep Analyzer under the mattress. Subjective sleep quality was reported daily via smartphone app. Salivary dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured on the final day of each intervention. Sleep data was available from 31 participants (mean age 69.8 years ± 5; 64.5% women). Although ISI improved after all intervention periods compared to baseline (estimated marginal mean ISI baseline: 14.44 points, inactive period: 12.37 points, active morning: 11.87 points, active evening: 12.35 points), there was no evidence for a difference in ISI between the active evening and active morning period (β 0.55, 95%CI -0.80, 1.91). compared to the active evening period, sleep midpoint occurred earlier during the active morning period (4:13 vs. 3:54 a.m. respectively, β 0.31 min, 95%CI 0.14, 0.48). No differences were observed in subjective sleep quality or DLMO. While morning vs. evening PA timing did not impact most sleep quality measures, it influenced sleep timing. Larger studies are needed to define optimal and personalized PA timing for improving sleep.

papers.title: Introduction to the special issue on RBD 40 years old: Perspectives on extensive clinical and research intersections.
papers.abstract: This Introduction to the special issue in Sleep Medicine marking the 40th anniversary of the first publication on REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in 1986 provides a brief historical background with early timelines, followed by current RBD and REM-without-atonia diagnostic considerations; and updates on RBD global epidemiology, RBD in younger populations, and the spectrum of RBD comorbidities and biomarkers. Other topics covered include RBD gut microbiome dysbiosis, proteome abnormalities, and neuroinflammation; RBD international research consortia; RBD economic burden and adverse quality of life; and neurodegeneration risk disclosure for newly diagnosed idiopathic/isolated RBD patients. Thirty-four RBD clinical and research intersections are depicted in a figure. Two recent review articles are cited that identified more than 4200 peer-reviewed journal articles published to date on RBD. The six articles contained in this special RBD issue cover animal models and basic science; genetics; pathogenesis; measurement and diagnosis; neurodegeneration, neuroimaging, and phenoconversion biomarkers; and cognition. RBD epitomizes the close collaboration and cross-fertilization of clinical and basic science research.

papers.title: Virtual EEG channel inference from four frontal electrodes for wearable EEG augmentation.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate a compact method for inferring virtual EEG channels from four frontal electrodes, with attention to both waveform fidelity and spectral-topographic usability. FAVC Net estimates 13 target channels from Fp1, Fp2, F7, and F8 using shared multi-scale encoding, source-state embeddings, target-conditioned signed source-block mixing, GATv2 refinement, attention-consistent skip fusion, and a waveform-spectral reconstruction objective. Training was task agnostic. Evaluation on PRED+CT used five independent subject-level splits and included neural and interpolation baselines and checkpoint-only source-perturbation tests. The complete FAVC-Net configuration achieved waveform fidelity comparable to the strongest waveform baseline, alongside lower spectral errors. Relative to the strongest non-FAVC comparator for each metric, log-spectral distance and PSD KL divergence were reduced by 30.50% and 38.94%, respectively. Under wearable-like perturbations, the most consistent advantages concerned spectral fidelity and channel-frequency texture, with condition-specific benefits in spectral-collapse measures. FAVC-Net provides montage-compatible deterministic conditional representations for low-channel EEG analysis. These representations transfer learned multichannel structure without adding independent measurement information beyond the recorded sources.

papers.title: Periodic limb movement disorder in adults: history, new research diagnostic criteria and a research agenda.
papers.abstract: Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD) has been recognized as a distinct sleep disorder since 1979, yet research has remained limited, partly because diagnostic criteria have changed substantially over time. These evolving definitions have hindered comparisons across studies and contributed to inconclusive evidence regarding the prevalence, clinical significance, and treatment of PLMD in adults. Without coordinated research efforts, PLMD risks remaining poorly characterized and surrounded by misconceptions. To reinvigorate research on PLMD, the International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG) appointed a task force to identify key barriers and propose practical solutions. After reviewing the historical evolution of PLMD diagnostic criteria and identifying persistent challenges, we aimed to improve diagnostic consistency and research applicability by developing Research Diagnostic Criteria (RDC) for PLMD in adults. These RDC reformulate core diagnostic elements: frequent periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS), clinically significant daytime or nighttime impairment, exclusion of key comorbid conditions (restless legs syndrome, untreated sleep-related breathing disorders, narcolepsy, and REM sleep behavior disorder), and demonstration of a causal relationship. We also propose a six-level classification system for graded reporting of PLMD status in research. Implementation of these RDC and the accompanying research agenda may help establish a stronger evidence base for PLMD.

papers.title: Post-COVID neurological manifestations are associated with neuroinflammation, increased autoantibody burden, and persistent complement activation.
papers.abstract: Neurological manifestations represent commonly persistent features of post-COVID conditions (PCC), but mechanisms underlying their pathogenesis remain unclear. In this study, participants with neuro-PCC (n = 29), mostly presenting with persistent headache, fatigue, sleep disturbances, anosmia/dysgeusia, cognitive complaints, and/or paresthesia, recovered from COVID-19 (n = 32), and non-infected controls (n = 32), all matched for sex and age, had paired serum samples from acute phase (0-14 days) and two time points of convalescence (3-6 months and 9-12 months) assessed for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens (ENA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and autoantibodies against cytokines using Luminex assays. Biomarkers of neuroinflammation, including neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), total Tau protein, and neurogranin were quantified by Ella ELISA and complement activation was determined by increased C5b-9 levels. Patients with neuro-PCC showed a greater number of neurological symptoms during acute phase, with increased frequency of headache and fatigue, and a higher prevalence of obesity and cardiovascular comorbidities. GFAP remained elevated for up to one year after infection, independently of symptom persistence. However, only patients with neuro-PCC exhibited a transient increase in NfL levels during acute phase, and persistent complement activation throughout follow-up. No specific autoantibody was associated with neuro-PCC, but these patients exhibited a higher cumulative autoantibody burden. Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that hospitalization and the neurological burden during the acute phase were associated with neuro-PCC, whereas anti-cytokine autoantibody counts showed an inverse trend. Increased complement activation and a higher autoantibody burden suggest a broad and nonspecific immune activation that may contribute to a sustained low-grade neuroinflammatory state, potentially driving the persistence of neurological symptoms after COVID-19.

papers.title: Late-timed eating alters the diurnal pattern of fuel selection and lowers metabolic flexibility without changing 24-hour energy expenditure: A randomized crossover trial.
papers.abstract: Meal timing may influence energy expenditure (EE) and metabolic responses. However, the effects of different meal-timing schedules on free-living physical activity, 24-h EE, respiratory exchange ratio (RER), and metabolic flexibility under matched energy intake and meal composition remain unclear. In a randomized two-period crossover trial, eight healthy young men were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either an early-to-late or late-to-early meal-timing sequence, with a washout period of at least 1 week between conditions. Participants followed each meal schedule for 7 days and stayed in a whole-room calorimetry chamber from the evening of Day 7 to the morning of Day 9. Identical meals were provided under both conditions, with matched energy intake, meal composition, fasting duration, and sleep-wake timing. Twenty-four-hour EE and RER were assessed from the morning of Day 8 to the morning of Day 9, while free-living physical activity and accelerometer-derived activity-related EE were assessed on Days 1-6. Accelerometer-derived estimates of activity-related EE during the free-living period did not differ between the early- and late-timed eating conditions (651 ± 112 vs. 656 ± 178 kcal/d, P = 0.922), and no significant differences were observed in 24-h step counts or time spent in different activity-intensity categories. Total 24-h EE did not differ significantly between early and late meal timing conditions (1879 ± 194 vs. 1856 ± 229; p = 0.489). Although the 24-h mean RER was slightly higher in the late-timed condition (0.895 ± 0.019) than in the early-timed condition (0.879 ± 0.017), the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.106, effect size d = 0.832). In contrast, RER during the sleep period (00:00-07:59) was significantly higher in the late-timed condition (0.897 ± 0.017) compared to early-timed eating (0.838 ± 0.027; p < 0.001). Moreover, the amplitude of 24-h RER variation-used as a surrogate for metabolic flexibility-was significantly lower with late-timed eating (0.131 ± 0.021 vs. 0.194 ± 0.030; p < 0.001). In this 8-day controlled meal-timing intervention, late-timed eating did not alter free-living physical activity or accelerometer-derived activity-related EE, nor did it alter 24-h EE measured in the room chamber. However, it was associated with a higher sleep-period RER and a smaller 24-h RER range, consistent with lower metabolic flexibility and an attenuated overnight shift in fuel selection from carbohydrate toward fat.

papers.title: DSGTANet: A semi-supervised dual-stream graph-temporal adaptation network for cross-subject continuous EEG emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Continuous emotion recognition using electroencephalogram (EEG) is a critical topic in brain-computer inter-faces (BCIs), with applications in mental disorder regulation and human-computer interaction. However, its practical appli-cation is significantly constrained by several key issues, including the scarcity of emotion labels, inter-subject distribution shifts, and heterogeneous regression noise. To address these issues, this study aims to develop a semi-supervised frame-work for accurate cross-subject continuous EEG emotion recognition. We propose a novel Dual-Stream Graph-Temporal Adaptation Network (DSGTANet). First, we collect an EEG dataset of six dynamic emotional transitions with continuous labels from 40 participants. Then, DSGTANet is designed to consist of a spatial structural stream, a temporal dynamic stream, and a reliability-driven fusion and alignment module. Specifically, the spatial structural stream learns robust EEG channel-topology features through a learnable graph structure, structural augmentation, and a self-supervised consistency constraint. Meanwhile, the temporal dynamic stream employs a Transformer to capture long-range temporal dependencies in emotion evolution and introduces label-conditioned domain adversarial learning with an exponential mov-ing average (EMA) teacher to enhance pseudo-labeling for unlabeled samples. Furthermore, the reliability-driven module explicitly estimates dual-stream predictive uncertainty via heteroscedastic regression and performs precision-weighted product-of-experts fusion along with reliability-weighted conditional distribution alignment. Experimental results on our constructed dataset and the public DEAP dataset show that DSGTANet outperforms state-of-the-art methods in valence and arousal regression, achieving superior accuracy and robustness. These findings highlight the considerable potential of the proposed DSGTANet for real-world EEG-based emotion decoding under conditions of limited labeled data and substantial subject variability.

papers.title: NCEL: Convolution-Enhanced Lightweight Neural Architecture for Robust EEG Signal Decoding in Noninvasive Brain-Computer Interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and clinical neuro-diagnostics due to its non-invasiveness and high temporal resolution. However, robust EEG decoding remains challenging, particularly for resource-constrained deployments. While lightweight architectures like EEGNet offer favorable parameter efficiency, their reliance on fixed convolution kernels and restricted temporal receptive fields inherently limits their performance in complex, highly variable scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a Neural Convolution-Enhanced Lightweight network (NCEL) that augments spatiotemporal EEG representations while preserving structural compactness. Specifically, a dynamic neural convolution module (NCM) is designed to learn input-dependent temporal filtering strategies for trial-to-trial variability and session-related distribution shifts.Furthermore, parallel multiscale temporal convolution branches are integrated to concurrently capture short-term local waveform transients and long-interval rhythmic dependencies. Finally, a lightweight channel-attention gating mechanism adaptively recalibrates intermediate representations, amplifying task-relevant neural responses while suppressing noise-dominated channels. Extensive evaluations on five benchmark datasets (BCIC IV-2a, BCIC IV-2b, ERN, SMR, and P300) demonstrate that NCEL achieves a mean classification accuracy of 82.75\% on BCIC IV-2b. Notably, NCEL achieves higher mean performance than the EEGNet reference values, with performance gains of 12.53 percentage points on the P300 dataset and 9.54 percentage points on BCIC IV-2b, while maintaining only $\sim$0.008M parameters. Additional subject-specific session-disjoint evaluations show comparable cross-session performance to EEGNet on BCIC IV-2a and a 1.80-percentage-point mean improvement on BCIC IV-2b. Overall, NCEL provides a parameter-efficient framework for resource-constrained EEG decoding, while broader cross-session generalization requires further validation.

papers.title: Physical activity partly inhibits autonomic imbalance, immune dysfunction and quality of life induced by chronic shiftwork in policemen.
papers.abstract: Chronic shiftwork can impair autonomic cardiovascular regulation and immune homeostasis. However, the interaction between occupational status and physical activity level in military police officers remains incompletely understood. This cross-sectional factorial study included 102 men stratified according to occupational status and physical activity level: physically active military police officers (PMP; n = 26), physically inactive military police officers (PMNP; n = 26), physically active civilians (CVP; n = 25) and physically inactive civilians (CVNP; n = 25). Quality of life, perceived stress, sleepiness, haematological parameters, cytokines and heart rate variability were assessed. Physical activity improved several Short-form questionnaire (SF-36) domains, particularly Physical Functioning and General Health. Military police officers demonstrated lower mean normal-to-normal intervals and lower high-frequency power than civilians, indicating differences in resting autonomic cardiovascular modulation associated with occupational status. Serum interleukin-10 concentrations were significantly lower in military police officers, whereas interleukin-2, interleukin-17 and interferon-γ did not differ significantly according to occupational status. Haemoglobin levels and platelet counts demonstrated significant occupational status × physical activity interactions. Perceived stress scores were lower in military police officers than in civilians. Chronic occupational exposure to shiftwork was associated with altered autonomic cardiovascular regulation and immune regulation in military police officers. Regular physical activity improved quality of life somewhat; however, several physiological alterations remained predominantly associated with occupational status, reinforcing the importance of occupational strategies targeting circadian health and physiological resilience. These findings highlight the physiological complexity of chronic shiftwork exposure in tactical occupational populations.

papers.title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

papers.title: Age-Adjusted Exploratory Analysis of Spectral, Aperiodic, and Microstate EEG Features in Multiple Sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can characterize functional brain alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS), but many EEG features vary with age. We therefore examined resting-state EEG associations with MS using age-adjusted models while explicitly accounting for the severe age imbalance in the available dataset. Resting-state 128-channel EEG data from the BrainLat dataset were analyzed. Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately to five global spectral/aperiodic tests, 16 global microstate tests, and the 128 channel-wise tests within each feature. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. After correction, diagnosis coefficients were significant for global bandwidth (β = 1.928, q = 0.0287), global aperiodic offset (β = 1.816, q = 3.29 × 10⁻⁷), and offset at all 128 channels (β range = 1.52-2.41; q range = 3.56 × 10⁻⁸ to 7.43 × 10⁻⁵). Global central frequency, exponent, PSD, and all 16 microstate measures did not survive FDR correction. No within-MS continuous-age or age-stratified result survived FDR correction. Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. The findings are exploratory and require age-matched replication with detailed clinical, vigilance, site, sex, and MRI characterization.

papers.title: "Tired but wired" - First-time parents lived experiences of sleep loss, tiredness and wellbeing during the first six months postpartum.
papers.abstract: Sleep loss is a common experience amongst first-time parents and can result in postpartum fatigue. There is a lack of research on first-time parents' lived experiences of sleep and sleep loss, and its associated effects on mental health, parental relationships, and overall wellbeing as new parents. We examined first-time parents' perceptions, experiences and attitudes to sleep loss, tiredness and wellbeing during the first six months postpartum in Ireland. One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted with fourteen first-time parents (female n = 10, male n = 4) from October to December 2025. The interviews took place online. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes were identified: 1) the gendered experience of sleep as a new parent, 2) (in)ability to sleep, 3) postpartum wellbeing struggles and 4) resilience and adapting. These themes highlighted how first-time parents navigate their sleep in their new role as a mother or father, their difficulty getting adequate sleep, complex wellbeing struggles as a result of sleep loss, and the discovery of new ways to function when dealing with sleep loss in the postpartum period. These findings highlight the need for healthcare professionals to recognise postpartum sleep loss as both a physiological and psychological experience, and to incorporate holistic, routine discussions of sleep into postnatal care.

papers.title: Dexmedetomidine effects on metabolic rate over 5 days in humans.
papers.abstract: The alpha-2-adrenergic agonist drug dexmedetomidine induces sleep-like sedation and reduces global metabolic rate. Drug-induced metabolic suppression sustained over days in humans could be a strategy for reducing energy expenditure (EE), oxygen consumption (VO2), and carbon dioxide production (VCO2) during prolonged rescue or austere conditions with limited life-support. We tested the feasibility of reducing EE, VO2 and VCO2 measured with intermittent indirect calorimetry using subcutaneous infusion of dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg/hour for 18 hours per day over five days in healthy adults. Five participants received multiple days of dexmedetomidine in a laboratory setting, and five separate participants received placebo for one or five days. Relative to resting metabolic rate, dexmedetomidine infusion reduced VO2 (effects, 95%CI, at 6-hour time epoch: -0.084 L/min, -0.145 to -0.023), VCO2 (-0.067 L/min, -0.130 to -0.005) and EE (-577 kcal/day, -1016 to -137). Relative to placebo, dexmedetomidine produced light sedation (Richmond Agitation Sedation Score: -1.25; 95%CI -1.70 to -0.80 relative to placebo), with lower heart rate (-15 beats/minute; 95%CI -23 to -7) and core body temperature (-1.3ºC; 95%CI -1.7 to -0.8). Dexmedetomidine effects on all physiological variables decreased over time and were absent after day 2. Maximum and minimum plasma drug levels did not change over days. Participants reported rebound anxiety and insomnia after the study. Administering a sedating level of dexmedetomidine that reduces VO2, VCO2, and EE for 2 days was feasible in healthy adults. However, tolerance to drug effects develops by 3 days, which is a critical limitation for long-term use of this drug regimen.

papers.title: Reduced cognitive empathy and differences in EEG activity in low-achieving adolescents.
papers.abstract: Students with low academic achievement tend to display more maladaptive behaviours in interactions with peers and teachers. Empathy plays a key mediating role in these interactions and is also linked to academic performance. In particular, facial emotion recognition is one component of socioemotional processing that may contribute to empathic responding. To explore the relationship between empathy, emotion recognition, and academic achievement, a comparative study was conducted with 40 students aged 14-17, divided into two groups: one with low academic achievement enrolled in a school support programme, and a control group with adequate academic performance. A multimethod approach was applied, including the Basic Empathy Scale, a facial expression recognition test, and electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings. Results showed significantly lower cognitive empathy in the low-achieving group in the primary between-group analysis. The overall between-group difference in facial emotion recognition accuracy was not statistically significant. EEG analyses identified exploratory between-group differences in source-level oscillatory activity estimates during facial-expression processing.
