papers.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Cognitive diseases/disorders are a major cause of disability affecting millions of people worldwide due to pathologies or conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, vascular cognitive impairment, and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The effects of these diseases/disorders can range from subjective cognitive complaints to mild cognitive impairment and even dementia that can affect multiple cognitive domains, causing disability and alterations in daily functioning and quality of life. Cognitive training has been researched as a potential therapeutic option for treating cognitive disability. In particular, cognitive training delivered using brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) represents a promising technology for cognitive rehabilitation. For this reason, this work presents a narrative review aimed at bridging the clinical aspects of cognition performance and the technical features of BCI systems. Additionally, it reports on the current advances of BCIs for cognitive rehabilitation in the pathologies/conditions that are the main contributors of cognitive impairment globally. Specifically, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment, cerebrovascular diseases, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder were included in the review; other pathologies that can also cause cognitive impairment such as multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, infectious diseases, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia or autism spectrum disorder, or drug or toxin-related causes were outside the scope of the present review. Across the literature, studies have reported that BCI cognitive training can improve cognition performance for mild cognitive impairment, stroke, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, showcasing its feasibility as a complementary therapy. However, the amount of evidence is still scarce, with few reported randomized controlled clinical trials and all of the applications comprising non-invasive systems using electroencephalography, while invasive or other non-invasive approaches remain largely unassessed. Therefore, further research regarding the design of BCIs for targeting specific cognitive domains is necessary to allow for the future introduction of these types of systems into clinical rehabilitation environments, rather than only demonstrating their feasibility, as has been mainly done to date.

papers.title: A Knowledge Transfer Method from Multi-Channel to Single-Channel EEG Toward Real-World Emotion Recognition Deployment.
papers.abstract: Multi-channel electroencephalography (EEG) provides spatial information for emotion recognition but requires more complex signal acquisition than single-channel EEG. This study proposes a multi-channel-to-single-channel knowledge transfer framework that uses multi-channel recordings during training and one selected physical EEG channel at inference. A 32-channel teacher is pretrained, and Sparsemax-based gating is jointly optimized with a student using classification, logits distillation, frequency-band consistency, and gating regularization losses. The frequency-band objective compares signal-level spectral statistics of the multi-channel recordings and the gated surrogate input. After channel locking, the student is retrained on the selected physical signal. Binary Arousal and Valence classification was evaluated on DEAP using 32-fold leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The proposed achieved higher subject-averaged balanced accuracy and F1-score than Channel-matched CE in both tasks, although component effects varied across tasks and metrics. These findings support the evaluated training approach under single-channel input constraints and provide a methodological basis for simplifying EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Physiology-Informed Blink Artefact Detection from Bilateral Frontal EEG Under Asymmetric Interference.
papers.abstract: Eye blinks contaminate frontal electroencephalography (EEG), while asymmetric disturbances can cause false detections. We present a physiology-informed detector that combines waveform correlation, peak-time agreement, amplitude similarity, and symmetric-component dominance in an explicit event-verification rule. It uses two frontal channels without supervised model fitting. Evaluation on raw ZuCo 1.0 recordings included 260 eligible blocks from 12 participants, totalling 1291.61 min and 8611 eye-tracker reference intervals. Scalp and periocular pairs were evaluated separately. On the scalp pair, participant-mean precision was 0.731, recall 0.774, F1 0.734, and false positives 1.469 per minute. At fixed settings, false-positive rates were lower than with single-channel thresholding and bilateral averaging (both Holm-adjusted p = 0.005859), and remained lower than those of four rule-based controls across five perturbation conditions. Threshold-selected simple controls achieved higher precision at similar recall. Component ablations quantified the effects of the verification checks on sensitivity and false positives. The offline Python detector required a median of 2.13 ms per minute of recorded data on an Apple M1 Pro. These results establish a computationally inexpensive approach that makes blink-event decisions directly inspectable through bilateral signal measurements.

papers.title: Triaxial Accelerometry Sensor for Respiratory-Effort Phase Landmark Detection During Sleep: A Cross-Modal Weak Supervision Approach.
papers.abstract: Reliable respiratory phase sensing is important for respiratory-synchronized hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HGNS), but conventional sensing approaches may impose additional burden. This pilot study investigated whether a surface triaxial accelerometry sensor (TAS) could detect thoracic respiratory inductance plethysmography (RIP) troughs, which were used as operational phase landmarks representing the transition from end expiration to subsequent inspiration, rather than as directly established physiological respiratory onsets. Ten participants underwent synchronized overnight polysomnography and surface TAS recording, providing 5377.3 min of analyzable data and 75,499 automatically generated RIP landmarks. Two complementary Conformer models were trained using Gaussian weak labels and combined using multi-offset dual-conformer fusion. Generalization was evaluated using outer leave-one-subject-out validation, with fusion weights and event thresholds selected from training-side validation data. At a ±1.0 s matching tolerance, the fusion achieved participant-mean precision, recall, and F1 scores of 0.78, 0.82, and 0.80, respectively, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.75-0.85 for the mean F1 score. It outperformed each component model in 9 of 10 participants; however, its F1 gain over otherwise identical single-grid fusion was 0.0036, below the prespecified exploratory advancement margin. These findings provide preliminary evidence that surface TASs can recover an RIP-trough-derived operational phase landmark in unseen same-center participants. Independent multimodal adjudication, external replication, and full-night causal testing are required before clinical or respiratory-synchronized HGNS applications.

papers.title: Multimodal Prodromal Patterns Associated with COPD Exacerbations in Home Telemonitoring: An Exploratory Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Characterizing multi-parameter physiological, acoustic, and environmental changes before acute chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations (AECOPD) is crucial for improving home telemonitoring and enabling timely clinical intervention. In a 12-month prospective observational exploratory pilot study (N=16), a multimodal Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem collected daily data on symptoms, lung function, cardiorespiratory dynamics, actigraphy, sleep, fine motor skills, bioacoustics, and indoor air quality. From 427 daily features across 4738 patient-days, collinearity mitigation retained 245 independent features. Linear mixed-effects models (LMM), nonparametric paired tests, and multi-timescale exponential moving average smoothing quantified prodromal trajectories and univariate discrimination during the 7-day pre-exacerbation window. Engagement analysis showed a dual hierarchy: passive background monitoring had high retention (>72 %), while demanding active tasks like peak flow spirometry dropped to 26.9 % compliance. Patients with frequent exacerbations showed higher reactive adherence. LMM frameworks identified a multisystem prodromal footprint marked by coordinated increases in cough frequency, sputum purulence, dyspnea, and resting heart rate. Acoustic measures showed notable pre-event changes in higher-order speech cepstral coefficients, voice-intensity variability, and cough spectral dispersion, providing objective proxies for airway limitation. Indoor environmental signals suggested domestic confinement but weakened after adjustment for macro-seasonal confounders. Multi-temporal kinetics demonstrated that acute physiological symptoms peaked within 72 h, whereas acoustic features required 3-to-7-day temporal smoothing (EMA3-EMA7) to optimize signal-to-noise ratios. In conclusion, these preliminary observations in the exploratory small cohort suggest that the transition from a stable baseline to the prodromal AECOPD phase is marked by a quantifiable, multi-systemic digital footprint across cardiorespiratory, bioacoustic, and symptom domains. Although requiring validation in broader populations, findings highlight the potential of multi-tiered digital health architectures that pair continuous passive sensing with low-friction active reporting to overcome task attrition and secure the uninterrupted longitudinal baselines needed for automated early-warning systems.

papers.title: Periodicity-Driven Adaptive Localization of Respiratory Regions for Non-Contact Respiration Monitoring in Sleeping Infants.
papers.abstract: Respiration is a critical vital sign for assessing the health status of infants during the first year of life. Conventional video-based respiratory monitoring methods often rely on manually defined regions of interest (ROIs) targeting specific anatomical regions, such as the chest or abdomen, or employ pretrained object detection models to localize body regions before extracting respiratory signals. However, in unconstrained sleep environments, infants may adopt diverse sleep postures, making it difficult to assume that respiration-induced movements will consistently appear in the same anatomical region or image location. To address this limitation, we propose an anchor-based respiratory-region localization framework that identifies spatial regions exhibiting prominent respiratory periodicity across the entire video frame without relying on predefined anatomical ROIs or separate body-region localization models. For each grid cell, time-series signals are constructed from inter-frame color/intensity variations and optical-flow-derived motion changes. The magnitude spectra of these signals are then multiplied element-wise to generate a respiratory periodicity map representing the spatial distribution of respiration-related periodicity across the frame. The grid cell with the highest Periodicity Score is selected as the Anchor Grid Cell and used as the primary respiratory region for respiratory-rate estimation. The proposed method was evaluated using 6-fold subject-wise cross-validation on 374 video clips from 15 infants. The single-Anchor Grid Cell approach achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.9953 breaths per minute (BPM), a root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.9681 BPM, and a Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.7287. Moreover, MAEs below 2.5 BPM were obtained for the supine, side-lying, and prone postures, indicating consistent estimation performance across the evaluated sleep postures. These findings suggest that respiration-related information in infants is not necessarily confined to predefined anatomical regions and may instead be expressed at different spatial locations depending on sleep posture.

papers.title: Beyond Local Gating: Toward Network-State-Dependent Neuromodulation.
papers.abstract: Brain stimulation is progressively evolving from anatomically targeted interventions toward individualized, adaptive, and network-oriented approaches. Recent developments in brain-state-dependent stimulation have demonstrated that neuromodulation can be optimized by synchronizing stimulation with ongoing neural activity, while adaptive cortico-cortical paired associative stimulation (ccPAS) has extended this principle to distributed cortical networks. However, current approaches continue to define brain state primarily through local electrophysiological features, such as oscillatory phase or power, even though ccPAS is specifically designed to modify communication between interconnected cortical regions. In this opinion paper, we argue that the endogenous variable guiding ccPAS should instead describe the instantaneous physiological state of the targeted cortico-cortical pathway. We propose that online source-space functional connectivity provides a biologically meaningful and technically feasible estimate of this pathway state, thereby enabling a new framework of network-state-dependent neuromodulation. As illustrative applications, we consider pathways spanning different levels of experimental characterization, from established sensorimotor interactions to the less-characterized ventral premotor cortex (PMv)-posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) pathway within the action-observation network (AON). This distinction highlights that the proposed framework is pathway-general, while its experimental implementation requires pathway-specific characterization of stimulation parameters and appropriate physiological readouts. In this framework, resting-state EEG is rapidly reconstructed in source space to estimate pathway connectivity, which is subsequently used to personalize stimulation targets and guide state-dependent ccPAS of a functionally defined cortico-cortical circuit. Finally, we discuss the technological prerequisites, methodological challenges, biological rationale, and open scientific questions that must be addressed before pathway-state-guided neuromodulation can be experimentally validated. We argue that redefining brain state as the instantaneous physiological state of the communication pathway targeted by stimulation may represent the next conceptual step in brain stimulation.

papers.title: RefineSleepNet: Task-Driven Signal-Domain Transformation for EEG/EOG Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging relies on effective representation of physiological signals. Representative raw-signal sleep-staging encoders typically transform input waveforms while progressively compressing their temporal resolution within the same encoding path. However, explicit modality-specific, sample-aligned, and task-driven signal-domain transformation before epoch-level feature extraction remains comparatively underexplored. To investigate this design, we propose RefineSleepNet, an end-to-end sequence-to-sequence framework that explicitly separates these two stages. Separately parameterized Signal Refinement U-Net (SRU-Net) branches first transform EEG and EOG waveforms while preserving the original temporal length, after which Epoch Feature Extractors (EFEs) extract epoch-level representations from the refined signals. Fused Sequence Attention (FSA) then performs multimodal integration and cross-epoch contextual modeling before epoch-wise classification. All stages are jointly optimized using the final sleep-staging objective without a separate waveform reconstruction target. RefineSleepNet was evaluated on Sleep-EDF-39, Sleep-EDF-153, and ISRUC-3 using subject-independent 10-fold cross-validation, achieving accuracy/macro-F1 (MF1) scores of 84.5%/79.8%, 83.5%/78.1%, and 80.3%/78.1%, respectively. Ablation experiments supported the coordinated design, while statistical analysis and intermediate-representation evaluations further examined the robustness and characteristics of the learned transformation. The learned transformation retained broad temporal and spectral organization while introducing local waveform changes and modality-specific spectral redistribution. These results support the staged organization as a viable modeling strategy for EEG/EOG sleep staging.

papers.title: Teamwork-Oriented Physical Education Course Organisation and Survey-Wave Differences in Physical Activity, Sitting Time, and Perceived Physical Literacy Among Medical Students: A Two-Wave Unlinked Parallel-Group Evaluation.
papers.abstract: Medical students face health risks associated with high academic demands and limited discretionary time, yet evidence remains insufficient on whether health-promoting strategies embedded within existing curricula can improve their health-related behaviours and outcomes. We conducted a non-randomised, two-wave unlinked parallel comparison within a compulsory physical education course. Across four survey cells, 354 questionnaire responses, rather than 354 unique longitudinal participants, were analysed. Physical activity and sitting time were assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form, perceived physical literacy using the Perceived Physical Literacy Instrument, academic burnout using the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey, psychological distress using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21, and sleep quality using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Differential changes were estimated using Group × Wave models. Relative to the comparison condition, the teamwork-oriented condition showed more favourable changes in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) (67.15 min/week, 95% CI 2.23 to 132.07; p = 0.043) and sitting time (-87.08 min/day, 95% CI -159.28 to -14.88; p = 0.018); BH-FDR-adjusted q values were 0.058 and 0.054. Perceived physical literacy showed a favourable but imprecise estimate (2.11 points, 95% CI -0.07 to 4.29; q = 0.058). No clear differential changes were detected for academic burnout, psychological distress, or sleep quality. The focal outcomes showed favourable estimated patterns, but none met the conventional 0.05 threshold after multiplicity adjustment. Given the non-randomised design, unlinked surveys, and complete confounding of instructor with course condition, the findings should be interpreted as differences between two specific instructor-course contexts rather than as causal effects of the instructional approach.

papers.title: Beyond Location Probability: Neural Correlates of Feature-Spatial Mapping Learning in Visual Search.
papers.abstract: Visual statistical learning enables humans to extract regular information from the environment, thereby optimizing the allocation of attentional resources. Previous studies have demonstrated that the visual system can learn the spatial probability of target occurrence and feature-specific spatial regularities for distractors. It remains unclear how target feature-location contingencies guide search when high-probability locations have equal overall target probability, or how such learning is reflected in ERP activity. The present study used a visual search paradigm that manipulated target-location probability and feature-spatial matching relationships, while simultaneously recording EEG data. Behavioral results showed that reaction times were significantly faster when targets appeared at feature-matched high-probability locations than when they appeared at feature-mismatched high-probability locations or low-probability locations. However, analyses by target feature showed that the feature-matching advantage was observed for color targets but not for shape targets. Electrophysiological results showed no significant differences in N2pc amplitude among the three conditions; when averaged across target features, LPC amplitudes were significantly smaller in both high-probability location conditions than in the low-probability location condition, but did not differ significantly between feature-matched and feature-mismatched high-probability locations when averaged across target features. These findings provide evidence that feature-spatial statistical regularities can influence visual search, while the feature-matching advantage was specific to color targets in the present study.

papers.title: Isotemporal Substitution Associations of 24 h Movement Behaviors and Creative Thinking in School-Aged Children: A Compositional Data Analysis.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined associations between 24 h movement behavior composition and creative thinking in school-aged children, using accelerometers, the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, compositional linear regression, and compositional isotemporal substitution analysis. A total of 319 school-aged children (168 boys, 151 girls; mean age = 10.06 ± 1.37 years; Grades 1-5) from Shanghai, China, were included. Relative time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA; β = 16.019, 95%CI [9.472, 22.578], p < 0.001) and sleep (SLP; β = 6.374, 95%CI [3.263, 9.492], p < 0.001) was significantly positively associated with total creative thinking scores, whereas sedentary behavior (SED; β = -11.621, 95%CI [-19.345, -3.906], p < 0.01) was significantly negatively associated; light physical activity (LPA; β = -4.284, 95%CI [-8.771, 0.207], p = 0.062) was negatively but nonsignificantly associated. Reallocating time from LPA or SED to MVPA or SLP was associated with significant increases in creative thinking, and reverse reallocations with significant decreases. These associations were asymmetric: scores rose gradually with the former reallocations but fell rapidly with the latter. For both MVPA and SLP, replacing SED yielded greater model-estimated gains than replacing LPA. These findings suggest that promoting creative thinking may benefit from an integrated approach to 24 h movement behaviors: increasing MVPA, ensuring sufficient SLP, reducing SED, and managing LPA. Time may be reallocated from SED and LPA to MVPA and SLP, while guarding against reverse reallocations. Future longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether reallocating time causally changes creative thinking.

papers.title: Problematic Smartphone Use and Occupational Balance Among High School Students: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Problematic smartphone use (PSU) may affect how adolescents organize and experience everyday occupations, yet evidence on occupational balance in school populations is limited. This cross-sectional study examined the association between PSU and occupational balance among 2681 students from six public high schools in Istanbul, Türkiye. PSU was assessed with the Smartphone Addiction Scale (SAS) and occupational balance with the Adolescent Occupational Balance Scale (A-OBS). The A-OBS total score was the primary outcome, and its four dimensions were secondary outcomes. In the common complete-case sample (n = 1573), the crude inverse association between SAS and total A-OBS was markedly attenuated after district adjustment and was not statistically significant in the fully adjusted model (B = -0.027, 95% CI -0.057 to 0.003; β = -0.055; p = 0.078). Small inverse associations were observed for Rest and Sleep (β = -0.086), Occupational Variations and Adaptation (β = -0.099), and Occupational Meaning and Value (β = -0.071), but not for Temporality; all three significant domain associations remained below 0.05 after Holm correction. Sensitivity analyses produced broadly similar patterns. Overall, PSU was not robustly associated with total occupational balance after contextual adjustment, while selected dimensions showed small associations requiring cautious interpretation and longitudinal confirmation.

papers.title: Smartphone Dependence, Sleep Quality, and Suicidal Ideation Across Adolescence: A Six-Year Longitudinal Study.
papers.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death during adolescence, and both smartphone dependence and poor sleep have been associated with suicidal ideation. However, it remains unclear whether these associations reflect stable differences between adolescents or year-to-year changes within adolescents. This study examined the developmental trajectories of smartphone dependence, sleep quality, and suicidal ideation over six years spanning the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and tested whether sleep quality accounted for the association between smartphone dependence and suicidal ideation at the between-person and within-person levels. Data were drawn from six annual waves (2018 to 2023) of the Korean Children and Youth Panel Survey 2018 middle school first-grade cohort (N = 2590; 54.2% boys). A parallel piecewise latent growth curve model (LGCM) and random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) were estimated. Smartphone dependence increased before the pandemic onset (B = 1.47 per year) and declined slightly thereafter (B = -0.16), sleep quality declined after the onset (B = -0.05), and suicidal ideation decreased before the onset (B = -0.10) and increased gradually thereafter (B = 0.03), with no immediate shift at the onset. In the LGCM, the indirect effect of smartphone dependence on suicidal ideation through sleep quality was significant for usual levels (B = 0.005, p < 0.001) and pre-onset change (B = 0.008, p = 0.001) but not for post-onset change (B = -0.001, p = 0.570); Wald tests indicated that the path from sleep quality to suicidal ideation (p = 0.001) and the indirect effect (p = 0.004) differed between the two periods. In the RI-CLPM, higher-than-usual smartphone dependence predicted higher-than-usual suicidal ideation one year later (β = 0.05, p < 0.001), whereas no within-person lagged paths involving sleep quality were significant. Smartphone dependence, poor sleep quality, and suicidal ideation thus co-occurred between adolescents, but annual within-person changes did not show a pathway through sleep quality. Because period differences cannot be separated from age-related development in a single cohort, they should not be interpreted as pandemic effects. These findings support attending to adolescents with high smartphone dependence and poor sleep within existing school-based screening systems, whereas the mechanisms through which risk is transmitted require studies with shorter measurement intervals.

papers.title: How Aesthetic and Economic Factors Affect Consumers' Purchasing Decisions: Evidence from EEG.
papers.abstract: Consumer theory identifies cultural and economic factors as key influences on purchasing decisions. Artworks, as material carriers of culture, are shaped by these factors in a particularly pronounced way. This study proposes that consumers' artwork purchasing decisions are jointly determined by aesthetic and economic considerations. Using event-related potential (ERP) technology, artworks were classified into a 2 by 2 matrix of aesthetic valence and price. Seventy students from a university in western China made purchase or rejection decisions while their electroencephalogram was recorded. Results showed that both aesthetic and price factors jointly influenced artwork purchasing decisions. Aesthetic valence had a larger effect (F(1, 69) = 134.98, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.662) than price (F(1, 69) = 22.47, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.246), and participants were most willing to buy positively rated, low-priced artworks (M = 42.2%, SD = 24.2). The medial frontal negativity (MFN) amplitude and theta-band power were larger during purchase than rejection decisions, and this difference was most pronounced when participants chose to buy negatively rated artworks (t(48) = 4.31, p < 0.001, d = 0.61). Because the sample was drawn from a single university in western China and consisted of young students, the conclusions carry generalisability limitations. This study maps aesthetic and economic considerations during consumer purchasing onto separable neural processes, contributing to the intersection of cultural neuroscience and neuroeconomics.

papers.title: From Exposure to Psychological Harm: A Socioecological and Trauma-Informed Narrative Review of Bullying, School Violence, and Youth Mental Health.
papers.abstract: Bullying and school violence are preventable exposures and potentially modifiable risk factors for adverse youth mental health and educational outcomes. This critical narrative review integrates epidemiological, longitudinal, genetically informed, quasi-experimental, meta-analytic, and intervention evidence on bullying, cyberbullying, selected forms of school violence, and their psychological sequelae. The evidence base available at the original submission was reassessed during revision through a complete structured rerun of PubMed/MEDLINE, APA PsycINFO, ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Google Scholar, major publisher platforms, and authoritative organizational sources from 15 to 27 August 2026, followed by a final update on 8 September 2026; reporting was guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). Evidence supports robust associations with depression, anxiety, trauma symptoms, loneliness, sleep disturbance, self-harm, suicidality, substance use, and externalizing difficulties, although effect estimates differ in design, metric, and certainty. We propose an evidence-informed, not prospectively validated, mechanism-to-action framework. Within the reviewed corpus, direct prospective mediation evidence was identified for interpersonal distrust and school belonging; longitudinal evidence supports a rumination-sleep sequence; and threat appraisal, humiliation/shame, and social defeat remain theory-supported candidate mechanisms. Socioecological theory organizes influences across individual, peer, school, family, community, policy, and digital levels. Trauma-informed principles are used as an interpretive and ethical lens; evidence for whole-school trauma-informed models remains limited. Whole-school anti-bullying programs modestly reduce exposure, but average effects on internalizing symptoms are small and heterogeneous. Systems should therefore coordinate exposure prevention with assessment, treatment, and follow-up of psychological harm. Progress should be judged by safety, equity, belonging, functioning, and recovery, not incident counts alone.

papers.title: Associations Between Interoceptive Awareness, Psychological State, and Physical Performance in Sport-Science Students: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Interoceptive awareness may support stress regulation in sport, but its association with objective physical performance remains unclear. This study examined relationships between self-reported interoceptive awareness, perceived stress, anxiety, sleep quality, and field-based performance in sport-science students. Eighty-five students (54 men, 31 women; 20.65 ± 2.43 years) completed the MAIA-2, PSS-10, STAI, and PSQI and performed handgrip, countermovement-jump, sit-and-reach, and bilateral Y-Balance tests. Analyses included Pearson correlations, Welch tests with false-discovery-rate correction, HC3-robust hierarchical regression, and exploratory age- and sex-adjusted bootstrap indirect-effect models. The MAIA-2 composite was inversely associated with perceived stress (r = -0.461, 95% CI [-0.614, -0.275], p < 0.001) but showed no detectable association with physical performance (r = -0.003 to 0.136; all q ≥ 0.961); equivalence testing indicated that four of the five performance correlations were statistically equivalent to zero within a ±0.30 bound. Women reported higher stress and anxiety, whereas men showed greater handgrip strength and jump height. Individual-sport participants reported higher state anxiety than team-sport participants (g = -0.886, q = 0.004). Interoceptive awareness did not significantly increase explained variance in any performance model, and exploratory indirect-effect confidence intervals all included zero. Self-reported interoceptive awareness was related to perceived stress but was not detectably related to brief field-based performance in this sample. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to test temporal and causal mechanisms.

papers.title: Trauma, Hyperarousal, and Sleep: Neurobehavioral Pathways in Affective Disorders.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common across affective disorders and may coexist with traumatic stress and persistent hyperarousal. This narrative review examines how trauma-related hyperarousal and sleep dysfunction are associated with major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD), while distinguishing observed associations from proposed mechanisms. A targeted search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified clinical, neurobiological, and translational literature on trauma, hyperarousal, insomnia, nightmares, circadian disruption, MDD, and BD. The evidence supports a multidimensional view of hyperarousal involving partly overlapping autonomic, cognitive-attentional, affective, and behavioral domains; however, it does not establish hyperarousal as a unitary mechanism or justify equating trauma-related vigilance with manic activation. Sleep disturbance may function as a symptom, vulnerability factor, or prodromal change, but no single sleep measure is currently a validated individual-level prognostic marker. Clinically, trauma history, sleep phenotype, affective state, comorbidity, medication effects, and current safety should be assessed jointly. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia and established trauma-focused treatments have the strongest clinical basis within their indicated populations, whereas imagery rehearsal therapy, prazosin, chronobiological strategies, and candidate biomarkers require diagnosis-specific and evidence-graded interpretation. Longitudinal studies integrating objective sleep measures and explicit temporal modeling are needed before proposed pathways or precision approaches can be considered clinically validated.

papers.title: A Component-Level Network Analysis of Emotional Symptoms, Sleep Problems, and Physical Activity Identity at a Chinese University.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study estimated a component-level network of depression, anxiety, and stress dimensions, sleep components, and physical activity identity among students at one Chinese university. Using convenience and snowball sampling, 3762 students at Zhejiang University completed the DASS-21, PSQI, and MIPAI-25. Regularized partial-correlation networks were estimated with EBICglasso (gamma = 0.50) using automatic correlation selection. Strength, bridge strength, signed bridge expected influence, and predictability were calculated. Network accuracy and stability were examined with 1000 bootstrap resamples, and sex differences were assessed using a Network Comparison Test with 1000 permutations. Scores above the prespecified screening cutoffs were observed for depression (76.0%), anxiety (79.5%), stress (62.8%), and poor sleep quality (80.2%). In the DASS-PSQI network, hypnotic medication use had the largest overall strength point estimate (1.126), whereas depression and anxiety subscales had the largest bridge-strength point estimates (0.121 and 0.093). In the exploratory three-domain network, hypnotic medication use again had the largest strength estimate (1.131); MIPAI acknowledgment had the highest bridge-strength point estimate (0.134), closely followed by depression (0.130), and remained the highest-ranked MIPAI dimension in the mixed graphical model. Its individual cross-domain edges were small, and their specific pattern was model-dependent. Overall network structure did not differ significantly by sex (M = 0.087, p = 0.117), whereas global strength was higher in males than females (7.11 vs. 6.83; p = 0.012); no individual edge remained significant after Holm correction. These findings describe cross-sectional conditional associations and do not establish causal or protective effects.

papers.title: Breathing-Practice Status and Psychological Outcomes 12 Months After a Structured Program in University Students.
papers.abstract: Evidence regarding long-term breathing-practice maintenance and associated psychological outcomes remains limited. This observational longitudinal follow-up examined psychological outcomes and self-reported breathing-practice status 12 months after a structured program in university students. Thirty-four students from the intervention group of a 14-week breathing study were assessed immediately after the program (T1) and at the 12-month follow-up (T2). At T2, 18 reported occasional or regular practice, and 16 reported no or rare practice. All 13 psychological outcomes were included in the longitudinal analyses. For each outcome, the T2 score was regressed on the corresponding T1 score and T2 practice group using HC3 robust standard errors. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied across all 13 outcomes. Compared with the no/rare-practice group, the ongoing-practice group had more favorable T2 scores for subjective happiness, general happiness, positive affect, sleep quality, all six dimensions of psychological well-being, and life satisfaction after adjustment for the corresponding T1 scores; all q < 0.001. However, the ongoing-practice group also had higher worry scores (adjusted difference 4.52, 95% CI 1.44 to 7.60; q = 0.006). Negative affect did not differ between groups (-0.50, 95% CI -3.51 to 2.50; q = 0.735). Sensitivity analyses produced the same pattern. Ongoing breathing practice was associated with several favorable psychological outcomes at 12 months, but also with higher worry scores and no difference in negative affect. Because practice status was self-selected and measured concurrently with the outcomes, these findings are associative rather than causal and may be influenced by common-method bias, recall bias, and social-desirability bias.

papers.title: Psychological Profiles, Stress, Sleep Quality, and Psychological Risk Indicators Across Teams and Competitive Levels in Elite Football Players.
papers.abstract: Psychological factors and sleep quality are relevant to athlete well-being and adaptation in high-performance sport, yet their distribution within the same elite football structure remains insufficiently understood. This pooled cross-sectional study described and compared psychological profiles and psychological risk indicators across 11 teams within a single elite football organisation and explored selected contextual variables. Participants were 376 elite football players (245 male and 131 female; aged 14-37 years) from teams competing at U16, U19, amateur, and professional levels. Assessment followed the Psycholight framework and incorporated selected dimensions from the CPRD, MIPS, STAI, DASS-21, and PSQI. Group differences were examined using nonparametric comparisons, Wilcoxon effect sizes, Fisher's exact tests, and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Psychological profiles and risk distributions varied across the studied teams, with heterogeneous patterns across psychological and sleep-related indicators. Given the close interrelationship between sex, age, team, competitive level, and season, these findings should be interpreted as patterns observed among the teams represented in the present sample rather than as independent effects of sex or competitive level.

papers.title: Identification of CLOCK and MARK2 as Candidate Blood-Based Biomarkers in Type 2 Diabetes: An Integrated Bulk and Single-Cell Transcriptomic Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is often accompanied by nervous system complications. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying T2DM remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify candidate blood-based biomarkers associated with T2DM by screening a neural-related gene set through integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis of peripheral blood. The present analysis focused on the systemic expression patterns of the selected genes in peripheral blood as indicators of T2DM-associated immunometabolic dysregulation, rather than on neurological involvement. The neural-related gene set was used only as a predefined screening starting point. Methods: We employed a three-tier validation framework comprising (1) a training cohort (GSE15932, 8 T2DM patients vs. 8 controls) for biomarker discovery using differential expression analysis and machine learning (XGBoost, random forest, and PPI network topology); (2) an independent validation cohort (GSE184050, 50 T2DM patients vs. 65 controls) for cross-dataset diagnostic performance assessment (ROC analysis); and (3) an experimental validation cohort (5 T2DM patients vs. 5 controls) for independent clinical confirmation by RT-qPCR. Additionally, single-cell RNA sequencing (GSE268210) was used to investigate cell type-specific expression and immune regulatory networks. Results: By combining multiple screening methods and cross-dataset validation, we identified CLOCK and MARK2 as key candidate genes from the neural-related gene set. CLOCK and MARK2 showed high discriminatory performance in the discovery cohort, whereas their AUCs were 0.613 and 0.653, respectively, in the validation cohort, indicating limited standalone discriminatory ability. Both genes are highly expressed in peripheral blood monocytes and are associated with MIF-(CD74+CXCR4)-mediated cell communication, TNFA-NFκB inflammatory signaling, and activation of oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Finally, RT-qPCR in clinical samples confirmed that both genes were indeed upregulated (p < 0.05). Conclusions:CLOCK and MARK2 were identified as candidate T2DM-associated blood-based biomarkers with reproducible expression differences across datasets. Their discriminatory performance was more modest in the independent validation cohort, indicating limited standalone diagnostic utility. Single-cell and computational analyses further suggested potential immunometabolic relevance. Because neurological phenotyping, cognitive assessment, and direct measures of nervous system involvement were not available in this study, any relationship between these genes and the neurological manifestations of T2DM remains speculative and hypothesis-generating, and requires prospective validation in cohorts with matched neurocognitive data.

papers.title: Ubiquitin Proteasome System BTB-Adaptor Protein Insomniac Modifies Seizure Severity and Response to the Ketogenic Diet in a Drosophila Model of Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) serves critical cellular homeostatic functions that contribute to neurological health, including neuronal metabolism, synaptic plasticity, and the molecular circadian clock. The UPS is tightly regulated to ensure the correct balance of healthy proteins and those targeted for degradation and recycling; malfunction in this quality control process can contribute to disease states such as neurodegeneration and cancer. Target specificity in this system is due in part to ubiquitin ligase adaptor proteins, such as those of the BTB superfamily of proteins, which connect substrates to the larger proteasomal complex. In Drosophila, the BTB family member insomniac (human orthologs KTCD2, 5, and 17) has been shown to regulate sleep, arousal, and synaptic plasticity, but has not been examined for a role in neuronal excitability disease phenotypes. Methods: We utilized a genetic approach to interrogate neurobehavioral dysfunction in mitochondrial encephalomyopathy (ME) and the ability of dietary therapy to modulate this dysfunction. Results: Here, we report that genetic interference with insomniac modifies seizure-like behavior in a neuronal-subtype-specific manner in the ATP61 model of ME, ameliorating seizure severity when knocked down in GABAergic or dopaminergic neurons. Furthermore, while ATP61 typically responds to ketogenic dietary therapy with a robust reduction in seizure phenotype, we report that knockdown of insomniac or its binding partner Cullin RING Ligase 3 (Cul3) in neurons ablates this effect entirely, a previously unreported role for the UPS in downstream neurophysiological effects of the KD. Conclusions: These results implicate UPS BTB adaptor proteins as therapeutic targets in seizure pathology and identify them as a novel contributor to the ketogenic suppression of neuronal hyperexcitability. These two neurological roles are likely to be proceeding via cellular and molecularly distinct pathways, including a non-CRL3-based mechanism of seizure modulation.

papers.title: Divergent Intralesional Enhancement Kinetics in a Primary Ovarian Leiomyoma on Dual-Layer Spectral CT: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Indeterminate solid adnexal masses can remain difficult to characterize on conventional CT. Dual-layer spectral CT provides iodine concentration (IC), effective atomic number (Zeff), and electron density relative to water (EDW) from the same acquisition. We report a histopathologically confirmed primary ovarian leiomyoma and describe its regional multiphasic spectral behavior. Case Presentation: A 37-year-old woman presented with an O-RADS 4 solid right adnexal mass. Retrospective analysis sampled two enhancement-defined intralesional compartments across true noncontrast (TNC), arterial, venous, and delayed phases. On TNC images, ROI-A and ROI-B showed closely similar Zeff (7.39 vs. 7.37) and EDW (103.8% vs. 103.9%). ROI-A showed intense arterial enhancement (102.2 HU; IC 2.95 mg/mL; Zeff 8.78) followed by decline, whereas ROI-B showed low early enhancement and marked delayed fill-in, with delayed values slightly exceeding ROI-A (83.8 vs. 71.3 HU; IC 1.74 vs. 1.54 mg/mL; Zeff 8.25 vs. 8.16). Initial histopathology suggested fibroma; immunohistochemistry established ovarian leiomyoma. Conclusions: The two enhancement-defined compartments showed closely similar baseline spectral measurements but divergent postcontrast behavior. EDW demonstrated substantially lower-amplitude phase-related changes than IC and Zeff. These findings are descriptive and do not establish a diagnostic spectral signature or histologic specificity. When multiphasic dual-layer spectral CT has already been clinically acquired, regional spectral analysis may provide quantitative characterization of intralesional enhancement heterogeneity. In this case, however, spectral CT did not establish the diagnosis or alter management, and definitive diagnosis remained dependent on histopathology and immunohistochemistry.

papers.title: Size Matters: A Large-Scale, Real-World Dataset of Smartphone-Based Obstructive Sleep Apnea Screening in the General Population.
papers.abstract: Background: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a highly prevalent sleep-related breathing disorder that remains substantially underdiagnosed and is causally linked to cardiovascular and metabolic morbidity. Clinical diagnosis relies on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) derived from polysomnography (PSG) or home sleep apnea testing. Low-threshold, clinically validated screening tools that can be used repeatedly outside a clinical setting may help to reduce underdiagnosis and to capture longitudinal information. Methods: We describe a real-world dataset generated by a medical device-grade, smartphone-only OSA screening application (Snorefox M) that calculates the AHI from nocturnal breathing sounds. All users who provided informed consent for the research use of their anonymized data between March 2023 and December 2025 were included. The diagnostic performance of the application had previously been validated against parallel PSG. Additional post hoc analysis of classification performance at additional AHI thresholds, together with the linear correlation between the app-derived and PSG-derived AHI are described. Results: The dataset comprises 239,132 measurements from 31,647 consenting adults. A total of 14,351 users contributed at least two valid nights, yielding 221,820 nights of longitudinal screening data. Across all attempted measurements, 96.5% yielded a valid analysis result. The mean per-measurement AHI was 14.3 (median 11.8, SD 11.0). Voluntary, self-reported demographic information was available for a subgroup of 8092 users (mean age 54.4 years, mean ESS score 7.2). Against PSG, the application detected moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥ 15) with a sensitivity of 0.91 and a specificity of 0.83, and severe OSA (AHI ≥ 30) with a sensitivity of 0.93 and a specificity of 0.97. The app-derived AHI correlated strongly with the PSG-derived AHI (Pearson r = 0.80, p < 0.001). The app-derived AHI discriminated against the PSG reference with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.951 for severe OSA (AHI ≥ 30), 0.925 for moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥ 15) and 0.877 for the AHI ≥ 10 threshold. Conclusions: This is, to our knowledge, the largest longitudinal dataset of unsupervised, real-world OSA screening from a general adult population using a clinically validated, low-threshold smartphone tool. Smartphone-based screening can complement established diagnostic pathways, support pre-clinical triage and generate longitudinal data not accessible through single-night testing, while self-selection and the unsupervised nature of data capture constrain representativeness. By introducing this resource, this work provides the basis for the in-depth analyses of demographics, symptom-result concordance and night-to-night variability.
